meta.display_title: Products for Home: A One-of-a-Kind Store and a WooCommerce [Checkout Funnel] Built to Sell
meta.summary: Products for Home sells Greek honey, olive oil and Gia Giamas fruit drinks to shoppers in the Netherlands and Belgium. We designed and built a storefront that looks nothing like a stock WordPress theme. Then we turned the buying journey into a WooCommerce checkout funnel. Every step, from product card to checkout, gives shoppers a reason to add one more thing.
meta.services: UI/UX & Brand Design, WordPress, WooCommerce, Web Development, Checkout Funnels
meta.challenge_statement: A single jar of honey rarely pays for its own delivery. The store had to [turn single items into full baskets], and look as special as the products it sells.
challenge_body: Products for Home is a Dutch web shop for Mediterranean specialities. It sells raw Greek honey from Samos, extra virgin olive oil and Gia Giamas traditional fruit refreshments. Beeswax candles and natural care complete the range. Orders placed before 15:00 leave the same working day, for customers across the Netherlands and Belgium.

The numbers behind it are those of every delicatessen online. Jars and bottles cost from a few euros each. Free delivery, however, begins at €60 in the Netherlands and €70 in Belgium. So a store like this lives on order value. Every visit has to end in a fuller basket rather than a single jar. At the same time, every extra click between wanting something and paying for it puts a sale at risk.

The store also had to look the part. These are sun-ripened, hand-picked products with a story on every label. Yet too many WordPress shops dress products like these in the same stock theme as everyone else. Products for Home needed the polish of a bespoke brand site. Behind the scenes, it had to run on WooCommerce, so the team could keep full control of products, prices and orders.
meta.constraints: One-of-a-kind design, Low-ticket products, Two free-shipping thresholds, Local payment methods, Full control in WooCommerce
meta.approach_intro: We skipped the off-the-shelf theme and built the storefront from our own library of custom Bricks elements. Then we designed the journey as one funnel, from the first product card to the last tick box before payment.
approach_body: Every section a shopper sees is a custom Bricks element we wrote for this store. That covers the header and hero, the product cards and product template, the reviews and the footer. One brand and UI system runs through all of them. Headlines use Playfair Display with one word in italics, while Outfit sets the interface. The palette sticks to sage, teal and deep petrol. We also built the elements to stay light. Each one ships its own small stylesheet and script, and LiteSpeed and FlyingPress serve the pages from cache.

Next, we mapped the funnel one step at a time and gave each step a job. Product cards sell straight from the grid. The product page answers price, payment and delivery questions at the button. The side cart shows how close the order is to free delivery and what goes well with it. And the FunnelKit checkout keeps one last, well-chosen offer between the shopper and the place-order button.
implementations: Bespoke Bricks element library: Designed and coded the storefront as our own Bricks elements, not a bought theme. It covers the header with its image mega menu and the hero slider with its scrolling text band. Category cards, bento sections, product cards, the product template, reviews and the footer complete the set. All of them share one brand system.

Conversion-led product experience: Built product cards with quick add, a wishlist and volume-discount badges. Our product template then puts tiered pricing right beside the add-to-cart button. Payment methods, same-day dispatch, the free-shipping thresholds and loyalty points sit there too.

Re-skinned side cart: Restyled FunnelKit's slide-out cart to match the store and added our own free-shipping progress bar. It tracks the Dutch and Belgian thresholds separately. Beside the basket, an often-bought-together column offers one-click add-ons.

WooCommerce checkout funnel with order bumps: Set up a branded one-page FunnelKit checkout with three delivery options and five local payment methods, including bol.checkout. An order bump waits at the payment step, and one-click add-ons sit beside the basket. A live review slider sits next to the total.
solution_body: The result is a bespoke WooCommerce store on WordPress, built around the basket rather than the single jar. Today, the live homepage opens on a three-slide hero for Gia Giamas, Greek honey and Greek olive oil. Floating product photography sits above a teal band of copy that never stops moving. Hovering Honing or Olijfolie opens a panel of image tiles, one per product family. Product cards then show their volume discount, a wishlist heart and a second lifestyle photo on hover. Their basket button adds the product without leaving the page.

From there, the WooCommerce checkout funnel keeps building the basket. On a product page, a staffelkorting table takes an olive oil bottle from €16.62 to €14.96 at three or more. It sits right above the add-to-cart button, with payment methods, same-day dispatch and the order's loyalty points underneath. Next, the side cart counts towards free delivery and suggests what shoppers often buy together. At the one-page checkout, shoppers choose home delivery, a DHL ServicePoint or collection in Alphen aan den Rijn. They can then pay in five ways. Just before the terms, a "Speciale aanbieding" offers a 750 ml olive oil for €15.75 instead of €17.50. One tick adds it. After the order, WPLoyalty points give shoppers a reason to return: one per euro, ten more per product review.
meta.outcome_statement: A storefront nobody mistakes for a WordPress theme, with a funnel that [sells at every step].
outcome_body: Every step of the journey now has a selling job. It starts with the badge on a product card and ends with the tick box before payment. At each stage, shoppers see the saving for buying more, the distance to free delivery and a well-matched extra. In the end, the WooCommerce checkout funnel is where the shop sees the effect in its sales.

The storefront keeps moving too. It runs on our own element library rather than a bought theme. As a result, new sections, products and offers go live on the same foundation. Meanwhile, we keep shipping improvements as an ongoing project with the Products for Home team.
outcome_pillars: A bigger basket at every step

features.title: Six details of a checkout funnel that [sells every day]

spotlights.title: A storefront that looks [nothing like] a WordPress theme
spotlights.problem: Shoppers buy Greek honey, olive oil and sun-ripened fruit drinks with their eyes first. In a stock theme, those products look like everything else on WordPress.
spotlights.built: We built the storefront from our own Bricks elements, not a theme. The hero rotates through Gia Giamas, Greek honey and Greek olive oil. Each slide brings its own floating product photography, with lemon and olive-branch cut-outs and progress dots around it. Beneath it all, a teal band keeps scrolling: "HEERLIJK VERFRISSEND • GEÏNSPIREERD DOOR GRIEKENLAND".

spotlights.title: Buy from the grid with [one tap]
spotlights.problem: Every page between interest and the cart costs sales. Worse still, a volume discount that nobody sees until checkout never changes what goes in the basket.
spotlights.built: Our product cards carry a STAPELKORTING badge wherever a volume discount applies. Each card also shows a wishlist heart, the star rating and the was and now price including VAT. On hover, a lifestyle photo swaps in and a round basket button appears. That button adds the product to the cart without leaving the page.

hotspots.label: Lifestyle photo swaps in on hover
Was and now price incl. VAT

spotlights.title: A buy box that [answers every doubt]
spotlights.problem: At the button, shoppers still have the same questions. Is it good? Is two cheaper than one? How do I pay, and when will it arrive?
spotlights.built: Our product template answers them in one column. The WebwinkelKeur score sits under the title. Next, a staffelkorting table takes a bottle from €16.62 to €14.96 at three or more. Then come the stepper and the add-to-cart button. Below them sit the payment methods, same-day dispatch before 15:00 and free delivery from €60 (NL) or €70 (BE). Finally, the column closes with the loyalty points this order earns.

spotlights.title: A side cart that [grows the basket]
spotlights.problem: A plain cart page is a dead end. It lists what's there but hides how close the order is to free delivery. It also offers nothing to go with it.
spotlights.built: We re-skinned FunnelKit's slide-out cart to the brand. Then we added our own free-shipping progress bar, which knows the separate Dutch (€60) and Belgian (€70) thresholds. Beside the basket, a "Vaak samen gekocht" (often bought together) column offers matching products with one-click Toevoegen buttons. Meanwhile, the coupon field stays folded away.

spotlights.title: A checkout with a [last-second offer]
spotlights.problem: WooCommerce's default checkout is long and generic. It also closes the door on selling more at the very moment a shopper is most ready to buy.
spotlights.built: We set up a branded one-page FunnelKit checkout with no menu to wander off to. It offers five ways to pay, from iDEAL | Wero to Klarna and bol.checkout. Below the payment options waits a "Speciale aanbieding" order bump. One tick adds a 750 ml olive oil for €15.75 instead of €17.50. Three more one-click add-ons sit beside the basket. Next to the total sit a trust column and a live review slider.

hotspots.label: Trust block next to the total

spotlights.image_alt: Products for Home WooCommerce checkout funnel: five payment methods, an olive oil order bump and a trust block beside the total

spotlights.title: Built for the [thumb] first
spotlights.problem: On a phone, image mega menus and wide product pages fall apart. A long list of honey types also turns into a guessing game.
spotlights.built: On phones, the menu slides in from the left with each product family as an accordion. Opening Honing shows "Alle honing" and a thumbnail for every type, so shoppers see the jar before they tap. The hero, buy box and side cart each get their own phone layout, with full-width buttons sized for a thumb.
